parakeet: The first point that I want to make in today's video is that religion is a delivery system, not the whole disease. Religion gives certainty a costume, it gives fear a choir, prejudice a pulpit, tribalism a sacred story. It gives control a divine signature. But the raw material was already human. And I think that matters because if we make religion the whole disease, we may miss the deeper human vulnerability that made religion so powerful in the first place. Religion didn't have to invent our fear of uncertainty. It didn't have to invent our discomfort with complexity or invent our impulse to divide the world into us and them, clean and unclean, good and evil or chosen and condemned. Those instincts were already in us. Religion learned how to organize them, how to ritualize them, sanctify them. Religion learned how to take ordinary fear and call it faithfulness. It learned how to take inherited prejudice and call it holiness, how to take control and call it order, to take suspicion of outsiders and call it discernment. And once those human instincts get wrapped in ultimate authority, they become much harder to challenge. Because now you're not just questioning a person's opinion, you're questioning their God. You're not just challenging a cultural norm, you're challenging the order of creation. You're not just asking someone to reconsider their bias, you're asking them to portray what they were taught as sacred. And that's what makes religion uniquely powerful, because religion can take common human weaknesses and place them beyond ordinary accountability. So no, I do not think religion is dangerous because religious people are uniquely broken. I think religion is dangerous because human beings are already vulnerable to simplistic thinking, borrowed certainty, fear-based belonging, and tribal morality. And religion can wrap those vulnerabilities in sacred permission. That's why religion can do so much harm, even when the people inside it think they're doing good.
